## Theoretical framework

Reading syllables, words and pseudowords aloud measures **written word recognition**: converting letters into sounds and accessing the word. It is the decoding component of the simple view of reading [@hoover1990simple] and the core of dyslexia according to the IDA definition (@sec-definicion).

**What distinguishes each list.** Dual-route models separate two procedures. The **sublexical route** converts graphemes into phonemes and is the only one that works for pseudowords. The **lexical route** recognizes the whole word, and it shows in words being read faster than pseudowords (lexicality effect) and frequent words faster than rare ones. In Spanish, children use both from Grade 2 [@avdyli2014lexical; @davies2013lexical]. That is why the platform has both lists: pseudowords measure pure decoding, and the difference with words estimates how much orthographic lexicon the child has built. Length (from one to four syllables) makes serial reading visible: the more the child depends on letter-by-letter conversion, the more each added syllable costs.

**In a transparent orthography, what discriminates is speed.** In Spanish, almost all children read accurately by the middle of Grade 1. Children with dyslexia are accurate but read more slowly, and their reading resembles that of younger children of the same reading level: it is delayed rather than deviant development [@davies2007spanish]. A meta-analysis of 79 European studies concludes that reading speed distinguishes readers with dyslexia in all orthographies and ages, whereas accuracy depends on age and transparency [@carioti2021depth]. In German, 70% of slow readers in Grade 1 were still slow in Year 8 [@landerl2008fluency]. That is why the score in these task sheets is **correct responses per minute**, not correct responses.

**What our data show.** These are the most reliable and valid tasks on the platform:

- **Reliability.** Stability between terms of ρ = .65 to .81, and 2021 α between .73 and .97.
- **External validity.** They predict low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency years later with a median AUC of .72 to .77 ([chapter](https://abarejo.github.io/leeduca-manual/criterio-woodcock.html), *in Spanish*). The longer lists (three- and four-syllable words) predict best.
- **Delay or deviance.** Comparing pseudowords with words among children of the same reading level separates delay from deviance ([Norms by reading level](https://abarejo.github.io/leeduca-manual/baremo-nivel-lector.html), *in Spanish*).

**Concurrent.** With other tasks in its own domain (Word and text reading), r = .62–.93. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Phonological awareness (5.2, r = .50); Phonological awareness (5.3, r = .60); Phonological awareness (6.1, r = .62); Phonological awareness (6.2, r = .60); Reading comprehension (6.3, r = .35); Phonological awareness (7.1, r = .44); Reading comprehension (7.2, r = .18); Reading comprehension (7.3, r = .23); Reading comprehension (8.1, r = .22); Rapid naming (RAN) (8.3, r = .31).

**Against reading difficulty and comprehension.** Against persistent difficulty, AUC .82–.94 (circular: agreement only). Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .55–.70.

Forms given at the same time point are compared. They are considered **equivalent** if the mean difference is smaller than 0.20 SD and the SD ratio is between 0.80 and 1.25. If the same children took them, **linear equating** is also computed, which puts the second form on the scale of the first, together with the correlation between forms (parallel-forms reliability). Besides its length, each word in the list is described by its **age of acquisition** (the age at which it is learned orally; norms by Alonso et al., 2015) and by its **orthographic neighbors** (words spelled almost the same; EsPal). The LEEDUCA platform task “Word reading: two syllables” (codes 1931, 71 and 73; LEEDUCA and DIS-ESP battery) assesses word reading (lexical route). The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 12 items. The time limit is 30 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 22 sessions, from 5 to 8 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .97 (N = 2,449, 12 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .79 (median of 18 session pairs; range -0.33–.91). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .46–.90. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .55–.70.
